name: Emeka Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior front-end developer at Carely, a company that makes an app for booking doctor and dentist appointments. Front end means the screens people actually tap on. Most mornings I'm fixing layout bugs, like a button that vanishes on older phones, and in the afternoon I pair with a senior called Marcus on bigger features. I cycle in along the canal, which is the best twenty minutes of my day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's for something useful. My gran used to struggle to get through to her doctor on the phone, and our app fixes that for some people. What wears me out is how much I still don't know, every code review shows me three new things. I use the AI chat now and then to explain error messages, but I don't let it write my code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a useful tool that got oversold, like a lot of tech. At work I'd joke that it can explain an error but it still can't tell you why the client changed their mind. Online I'd mostly keep quiet, there's enough noise already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's good for me. I'm still learning. A plateau gives me the years I need to actually get good, and the routine stuff it speeds up is mostly boring anyway. Renaming things, writing test data, that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep learning the craft properly. I'd use the AI chat a bit more for the tedious stuff, maybe set it up to write test data by the end of the year. And I'd ask Marcus if I can lead a small feature on my own by summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. A bit relieved for the whole industry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use the AI chat now and then. Would that change in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. Once everyone agrees it's just a tool, I'd use it like a spell checker, without thinking about it. But I'd still want to understand every line I ship, because someone's appointment depends on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your money or your home life that worries you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, I'm lucky. I've got about eight months of pay saved, and a small share of my late gran's house that my family rents out. My partner Sanna teaches primary school, so between us we're fine. If anything I'd worry about her class sizes more than my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to talk about who gets the gains. If one developer can do the work of three, the company shouldn't just pocket that. I'd say that in the team retro, politely, and less politely online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried. Coding is right there in the list, and I'm junior and still slow. My company Carely froze hiring once this year, and if the tools get this good, the company won't need people like me to do the screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd get serious about the AI tools, use them every day by spring, because the people who don't will go first. Then I'd join the tech workers' union branch that's been trying to start at Carely. And I'd look at jobs in the public health service's digital team, because public jobs change slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got money and time, so it's not panic. But I can feel the floor shifting under the exact bit of the job I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Carely do you think goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the juniors and the testers. There's a tester, Aisha, who's been there six years and does everything by hand, and I'd be worried for her. Me and the other juniors would be next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd join the union push. Your partner is a teacher. Has Sanna's union shaped how you see this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Completely. My partner Sanna's union got her school a proper agreement on class sizes. That's what made me think workers can actually set terms, instead of just reading the news and hoping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a proper safety net, and I'd mean it. Online I'd back anything that shares the gains, like a basic income or a shorter working week. At work, I think there'd be nothing to say, everyone would be updating their CVs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm out within a year of it arriving. Front end is pure screen work. Two years is nowhere near long enough for a junior like me to become the kind of senior they'd keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the holiday plans and keep my savings untouched. I'd sign up for a bike mechanic course in the evenings, because I already fix my own bike and it's hands-on. And I'd vote and campaign for whoever promises an income for people pushed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm the right age to be hit hardest, too young to have built anything and too old to start from nothing cheaply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI first, robots three years later. Where does that leave a front-end developer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nowhere, as a developer. The robots coming later gives hands-on jobs a few more years, so that's where I'd head. Fixing bikes isn't a fortune, but a robot that can true a wheel properly is a while off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if the pay stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out, the gym, the new laptop I've been eyeing. Then I'd talk to my family about the rent from my gran's house, whether it should come to me for a while. I'd feel awful asking, but that's what it's there for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned and we should act like it. I'd push the Carely union branch to negotiate retraining budgets now, before the layoffs start. Publicly I'd sound calmer than with the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still don't think there's a long future for me in front end. But five years is long enough to get one real step up the ladder and bank the money. Then I'd jump while I still had a choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to the public health service's digital team in the first year, because it'll change slower and it's closer to patients. I'd save an extra few hundred a month. And I'd start a part-time course in physiotherapy assistance in year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a working anxiety, if that makes sense. I'd be busy rather than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two years didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two things. I get to leave on my own terms instead of being pushed. And I can pick something better than a quick fix, something with people in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still head for bike repair, or something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with people. Bike repair is a hobby that would become a job out of panic. Helping someone walk again after an operation, I think I'd actually love that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade to build a fairer system, so let's not waste it. I'd be the annoying person at parties talking about shorter working weeks. Online I'd share good ideas rather than doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means I can have a proper career in software, maybe eight good years. I'd be in my late thirties when it arrives, with savings and options. That's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Carely and push hard to become mid-level within two years. I'd max out my savings while the pay is good. And I'd stay in the union, because rules for the decade after get written in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. Knowing the AGI is ten years off is like knowing your rent will go up in ten years. You plan for it, you don't lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people would say ten years is too far away to plan for. Is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the details, yes. For the direction, no. I know I'll need a second career, so I'd save like I need one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Sanna change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably buy a flat sooner rather than later, while we both earn well. And we'd talk about kids in five years rather than seven, so they're older when everything changes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be thrown out of the one thing I've trained for, before I'm even good at it. What would help is a public retraining fund that pays you while you learn, and a basic income floor so people aren't learning in a panic.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who people trust. I don't trust the companies to share the gains, but I do trust unions and schools, because I've seen my partner Sanna's union actually win things.

headlineQuote: I'd be thrown out of the one thing I've trained for, before I'm even good at it.
portrait: Emeka is a **27-year-old** junior front-end developer at a health booking app, still learning the craft.
He uses **AI chat** now and then and picks up tools once they're proven.
Savings and a share of a **family house** mean money isn't his first fear.
He trusts **unions** over companies, inspired by his teacher partner's wins.
With short warning he heads for **hands-on** work; with longer warning, a caring career.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing his trade before he's even good at it.
whatWouldHelp: A paid **retraining fund** plus a **basic income** floor.
